# Wisdom of Solomon Chapter 2 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Vaticanus, Wisdom 2 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/WIS_002_page_001.jpg

---

*[Here the author gives voice to the philosophy of the ungodly — a dark monologue that is powerful precisely because it is coherent]*

**2:1** They reasoned it all out, but they reasoned badly: "Our life is short and full of grief. There is no cure for death, no one has ever come back from the grave.

**2:2** We came into being by accident. When we are gone, it will be as if we never existed. The breath in our lungs is only smoke. The mind is just a spark from the rhythm of our heartbeat —

**2:3** put it out, and the body crumbles to ash. The spirit thins into air and disappears.

**2:4** Our very name will fade with time. No one will remember what we did. Our lives will vanish like a cloud's shadow, dissipate like morning mist scattered by the sun and melted by its heat.

**2:5** Our days are a shadow sliding past. There is no halting our end. It is sealed. It cannot be undone.

**2:6** So then — enjoy what is here. Use everything the world offers, with the intensity of youth.

**2:7** Drink expensive wine. Fill the air with perfume. Don't let a single spring flower go by without seizing it.

**2:8** Wreathe our heads with roses before they fade.

**2:9** No one left out of the celebration — let everyone have their share. Leave pleasure-tokens wherever we go. This is what life gives us. This is our lot, and there is no other.

**2:10** Let's crush the righteous poor man. No mercy for the widow. No deference for the white-haired elder.

**2:11** Our power is our only law. Weakness, by definition, is worthless.

**2:12** Let's keep a close watch on this righteous man — he's a walking inconvenience. He gets in the way of everything we do. He throws the law in our faces and accuses us of failing our upbringing.

**2:13** He claims to know God personally. He calls himself a child of the Lord.

**2:14** He's become a living challenge to everything we think. Even looking at him is unbearable —

**2:15** his whole way of living is different from everyone else's. His paths run in a completely opposite direction.

**2:16** He treats us like counterfeit coins. He steers around our way of life like it's contaminated. He says the righteous have a blessed end, and he goes around boasting that God is his father.

**2:17** Let's find out if any of this is true. Let's see what happens to him at the end.

**2:18** If this righteous man really is God's son, God will step in for him. God will pull him out of his enemies' grip.

**2:19** So — let's humiliate him. Let's put him through pain. Then we'll see just how gentle he is. We'll test that patience of his.

**2:20** Let's put him to death in the most degrading way possible. By his own logic, someone is looking out for him."

**2:21** That was their reasoning. They got it completely wrong. Their own wickedness had blinded them.

**2:22** They had no access to the hidden purposes of God. They couldn't see the reward waiting for the holy. They had no sense of the honor God reserves for those who are blameless.

**2:23** God made the human person for imperishability. He shaped us as an image of his own eternal nature.

**2:24** But death entered the world through the devil's envy. And those who take the devil's side will find out what that means.

---

*PNEUMA notes: The speech of the ungodly (vv. 1–20) is rendered as a genuine philosophical monologue — coherent, seductive, and dangerous. Its nihilism deserves to be felt, not softened. The short sentences build momentum. The pivot at v. 21 ("They got it completely wrong") is the author's sharpest rhetorical thrust. Verse 23's aphtharsia — "imperishability" — is deliberately maintained against mere "immortality," as it describes an ontological quality of the image of God, not just survival of death.*
